summary: SIP supports hop-by-hop traceroute of messages via Max-Forwards, and a separate mechanism exists for media loopback test calls. This document describes a way to do traceroute-style testing of the media path hop by hop.

plainLanguage.summary: Traceroute shows where a letter goes. This RFC lets you see where a voice or video stream goes by looping it back at each stop.

questions: how does sip max-forwards traceroute work
subtitle: Using SIP's Max-Forwards counter and media-loopback test calls to find where in a call's media path things break.

tldr.problem: When a SIP call crosses media-relaying B2BUAs and the audio or video goes bad, it is hard to tell which hop is at fault, and media loopback cannot target a B2BUA directly because it usually has no Address of Record.
tldr.mechanism: The caller sends media-loopback INVITEs to the real target with Max-Forwards starting at 0 and rising by 1. A supporting B2BUA that receives Max-Forwards 0 answers the call itself with a Reason header cause of 483.
tldr.outcome: The caller can test the media path to each successive B2BUA in turn. B2BUAs should control who can make such calls, because they use resources and could be a denial-of-service vector.

today: RFC 7403 is a Proposed Standard from November 2014. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Media Paths Need Tracing
sections.content:
In many SIP deployments the media does not flow straight from the calling User Agent Client (UAC) to the answering User Agent Server (UAS). SIP Back-to-Back User Agents (B2BUAs) in the signaling path often put themselves in the media path too, by changing the SDP. They do this to inject media such as music-on-hold, or to relay media for transcoding, IPv4-IPv6 conversion, NAT traversal, SRTP termination or media steering.

When media fails or degrades, it is hard to see where. A media-loopback mechanism exists in RFC 6849, but it cannot be aimed at a B2BUA directly: B2BUAs typically have no Address of Record (AOR), and it is not known in advance which B2BUAs a call will cross. Targeting them by URI also would not guarantee the same media path as a real call.

The RFC's answer is to call the real target, Bob, but make the call end at each B2BUA in turn using a traceroute-style counter.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message passes through many helpers and arrives garbled, you want to ask each helper to read it back to you. This RFC is how you do that for phone calls.

sections.title: The SIP Traceroute Mechanism
sections.content:
SIP can already do a simple request traceroute with the Max-Forwards header field. The sender starts at 0, gets a 483 Too Many Hops response from the next hop, then raises the value for each later request to reach devices further downstream.

This RFC uses the same approach for media. The caller (Alice) sends an INVITE to the target AOR (Bob) with Max-Forwards: 0 and media-loopback SDP based on RFC 6849. The next hop either rejects it with 483, or, if it is a supporting B2BUA whose policy allows the test, answers the INVITE and creates a media-loopback session.

Alice then ends that session and sends another INVITE to the same AOR with Max-Forwards 1, which reaches the second hop, and so on. Each answering B2BUA includes a Reason header with cause value 483 in its 200 response, until the INVITE reaches the final UAS, which does not use that Reason cause. The RFC also suggests uses such as a permanent test call across a SIP trunk between an enterprise and a service provider, or automated measurement systems.
sections.plainLanguage: First you ask the nearest helper to repeat your voice. Then the second helper, then the third. Each time you reach one step further down the line.

sections.title: What B2BUAs Must Do with Max-Forwards
sections.content:
Under RFC 3261, the UAS half of a B2BUA does not technically need to inspect Max-Forwards; only proxies do. RFC 7332 changed this so a compliant B2BUA inspects the value to prevent loops, and copies and decrements it as a proxy would.

The traceroute mechanism needs that behavior to work. So a B2BUA that supports it MUST also comply with RFC 7332.
sections.plainLanguage: Every helper has to count down the number as the call passes through, or the trick cannot work.

sections.title: Answering the INVITE
sections.content:
If a B2BUA gets a dialog-creating INVITE with Max-Forwards 0 and media-loopback SDP, and its policies allow it, it answers as if it were the original target. The normal SIP procedures and RFC 6849 apply.

In the 200 response the B2BUA MUST add a Reason header (per RFC 3326) with protocol SIP, cause 483 and reason text Traceroute Response. This tells the caller the call was answered because Max-Forwards reached 0, not because it reached the final UAS. When the ultimate target answers, no Reason header is added, and the caller knows the traceroute is complete.

If the B2BUA does not accept the session, for example because of local policy, it SHOULD respond with 483 Too Many Hops, just as it would without this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper that answers stamps the reply with a note saying I am only a helper. The last person in the chain does not add that note, so you know you have reached the end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Answering media-loopback calls uses resources on the B2BUA and network bandwidth, so it could be used for denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. B2BUAs should therefore offer options to control who can make such test calls, how many can run at once, and how long they can last. Deployers should set these to bring DoS risk to an acceptable level. For example, a B2BUA might require digest authentication with specific credentials, or allow only certain sources at a certain time. The RFC says such policies are vendor specific and cannot be defined in the document.

The security considerations of RFC 6849 also apply. Because B2BUAs have no human user watching loopback activity, B2BUAs should log such events or give some form of administrative notification.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could keep asking a helper to repeat things and wear it out, so helpers need rules about who can ask and for how long.
